name: Scrotal cooling / ball icing

card.summary: Chilling the testes with ice or cold packs to support sperm or testosterone; rooted in real testicular physiology but untested as a practice.
card.aka: ball icing, testicle cooling, cold exposure for testes
card.note: No studies found; excessive cold can injure skin, and the body already regulates scrotal temperature.

quick.overview:
Scrotal cooling, or 'ball icing', is a fringe practice of applying cold to the testes in the hope of improving sperm quality or testosterone. It draws on the established fact that the testes work best a few degrees below core body temperature.
No studies were found testing deliberate cooling in healthy men for these goals. Its logic is an extension of heat-and-fertility research rather than evidence for the practice.
quick.mechanism: The scrotum normally keeps the testes around two to three degrees Celsius below core temperature, adjusting with the cremaster muscle and dartos fascia. Proponents reason that extra cooling will help sperm production. Reference sources say heat impairs spermatogenesis but do not say that further cooling improves it.
quick.risks: Reported or plausible concerns include skin cold injury from direct ice contact and the cremasteric reflex that draws the testes upward in cold. The body's own regulation already maintains testicular temperature, and the effect of extra cooling in healthy men has not been studied.

lead: Scrotal cooling, informally 'ball icing', is a fringe practice in which men apply ice, cold packs or cold water to the scrotum, hoping to improve sperm quality or testosterone. It is discussed in biohacking and fertility-optimisation circles, on Reddit and YouTube, and occasionally on looksmaxxing forums.[9][10]

The looks connection is through testosterone: in looksmaxxing culture, higher testosterone is associated with muscle mass, leanness, facial and body hair and other masculine traits, so anything believed to support testicular function is of interest. Sperm quality is a related fertility concern rather than an appearance one.

The idea builds on documented physiology: the scrotum keeps the testes about two to three degrees Celsius below core body temperature, and higher temperatures affect spermatogenesis.[1][2] A 2013 systematic review found eight articles on scrotal cooling and spermatogenesis and reported insufficient evidence for firm conclusions, with a positive trend toward improved fertility.[4] Urologist Aaron Spitz told Mel Magazine that deliberate cooling can raise sperm counts but has not been shown to increase testosterone.[9]

angle.text: Practitioners apply cold to the scrotum to support testicular function, reasoning that testes work best slightly below body temperature. Published work on cooling concerns sperm and fertility; no study measures its effect on testosterone or physique.

paras: Practitioners describe brief applications of cold to the scrotal area using ice packs, frozen vegetables or similar items, often over underwear. Mel Magazine distinguishes the do-it-yourself practice from clinical cryo treatments sold for aesthetic purposes.[9] The rationale offered is that cooler testes mean better sperm production, extending the known effects of heat. Details vary by account.[9][10]

Mel Magazine, in a story dated June 2022, traced the trend to a YouTube fitness coach known as Vigorous Steve, who promoted it in a video about a year earlier, and to Reddit communities such as r/Testosterone and r/MorePlatesMoreDates where users trade routines and reported results.[9] The coach cited blood work he said showed higher testosterone after his protocol, and Redditors described stronger morning erections and more potent ejaculations, often alongside other habits such as ashwagandha and sun exposure, without presenting testosterone results.[9]

IFLScience covered the trend in October 2022 as a biohacking fad that had run for at least a year, quoting users who described mood, energy and libido changes and a urologist, Lye Diwa, who said no large clinical trials support icing for sperm count; the author suggested placebo and healthier habits might explain reported benefits.[10] Esquire India reported that longevity entrepreneur Bryan Johnson includes ice packs on his testicles during a morning sauna session as part of his published routine, which he frames as a contrast therapy; the article states that no high-quality human studies show icing raises testosterone, improves fertility or slows ageing.[11]

The scrotum holds the testes at about 35 C, a few degrees below the core temperature of 37 C. The cremaster muscle and the dartos fascia adjust the testes' distance from the body, and the scrotum usually tightens in cold.[1]

Another reference says sperm production is most efficient slightly below core temperature, with efficiency falling both below and above about 33 C, and that temperatures above roughly 36.7 C impede it.[2] In mice, brief scrotal heat stress caused DNA damage, reduced fertility and abnormal embryonic development.[2] A fertility reference reports that sustained high ambient temperature consistently lowers sperm quality in animals and links heat to lower sperm quality in humans.[3]
Leydig cells in the testes produce testosterone under pituitary luteinizing hormone control.[2]

Mel Magazine's account of the literature lists three older findings: cold sponging of the scrotum improved semen quality in three infertile men in 1954; nightly cold packs raised sperm density and motile sperm share in a 1984 report; and in 2005, eight weeks of nocturnal cooling with circulating-air pumps increased sperm concentration and total count in men with low counts and a history of testicular maldescent.[9] A 1982 clinical report likewise described testis hypothermia for infertility due to poor semen.[8]

Researchers have developed cooling products for fertility research, including a hydrogel scrotal cooling patch tested in a registered randomised controlled trial protocol of men with low sperm counts, and specialised cooling underwear.[6][7] In a prospective study of cyclic cooling underwear, median scrotal skin temperature was 34.6 C in the cooling period versus 35.3 C in the control period, a reduction of 0.7 C, which the authors described as feasible without impairing daily activities.[7] Esquire India notes these studies used mild wearable devices rather than ice packs.[11]

Spitz told Mel Magazine that testicles need to be about 2.5 degrees cooler than core temperature for sperm production and that icing is generally considered inconvenient and probably unnecessary rather than harmful; he advised avoiding hot water and noted that prolonged sitting and sleeping can raise scrotal temperature and that looser underwear may support sperm counts.[9] IFLScience quotes a urologist as saying no large clinical trials advise icing as a means to improve sperm count, while mentioning small studies linking cold to better sperm quality.[10]

General concerns include skin cold injury from direct ice contact; one user quoted by IFLScience names burns as the main worry and advises against placing ice directly on skin.[10] Vigorous Steve reported some testicular retraction after forgetting to remove an ice pack.[9] Reference sources also note that the cremasteric reflex raises the testes in response to cold.[2] Esquire India warns that repeated intense cold could damage tissue or reduce circulation.[11]

A 2013 systematic review of eight articles concluded there was insufficient evidence for firm conclusions on scrotal cooling and male fertility, while observing a positive trend, and called for well designed randomised trials.[4] A 2016 review of lifestyle and complementary therapies for male infertility described the data for scrotal cooling, along with acupuncture and several other therapies, as sparse or inconclusive.[5] A 1982 report described testis hypothermia for infertility due to poor semen.[8]
No studies were found of deliberate home cooling in healthy men for testosterone or appearance.

lore.intro: Cooling the testes appears in fertility and testosterone biohacking discussions as a counterpart to avoiding heat, promoted by YouTubers and Reddit users.[9]

claims.claim: Cooling the testes improves sperm production
claims.believers: Proponents reason that sperm thrive below body temperature, so more cooling should help.[9]
claims.experts: References report that heat impairs spermatogenesis and that efficiency falls both below and above about 33 C; a systematic review observed a positive trend for cooling but insufficient evidence.[2][4]

claims.believers: A YouTube coach cited blood work he said showed higher testosterone, and Redditors report better libido and erections.[9]
claims.experts: Leydig cell testosterone production is described as regulated by pituitary luteinizing hormone; a urologist said cooling has not been shown to increase testosterone and no studies of cooling on testosterone were found.[2][9]

claims.claim: Heat harms sperm, so cooling is protective
claims.believers: Practitioners cite heat-related declines in semen quality.
claims.experts: Heat is associated with lower sperm quality in humans and animals.[3]

claims.claim: Icing improves mood, energy and sleep
claims.believers: Users quoted by IFLScience describe improved mood, energy, libido and sleep.[10]
claims.experts: The IFLScience author suggests placebo and accompanying healthy habits may explain such reports; no studies examine these outcomes.[10]

claims.claim: Sauna plus testicle icing is a longevity strategy
claims.believers: Bryan Johnson includes ice packs during a morning sauna session in his published routine.[11]
claims.experts: Esquire India reports no high-quality human studies showing icing improves fertility, raises testosterone or slows ageing.[11]
